articles.title: ‘Gone in a blink’: Nepal floods sweep away Indian workers who built hotels
articles.summary: The migrants were at work, building homes and hotels, when the floods hit, sweeping three of them away.
articles.body:
Bettiah, India – Neyaz Miya was adjusting a kitchen handle. Mehadi Hassan was fixing a bracket for a bed.

They were at different construction sites – Miya in a half‑constructed home, a little higher up the hill, while Hassan was on the ground floor of Ganesh Hotel, closer to the Trishuli River that flowed through Syafrubesi, a bustling market town near the Nepal‑Tibet border, now wiped off the map by the August 26 flash floods.

More than 1,200 bodies have been recovered since then, at least 4,000 people remain missing, and more than 13,000 have been rescued.

“First came the terrifying loud sound. Then the ground trembled, and dark clouds descended upon us,” recalls 34‑year‑old Miya, who ran further up the hill with his phone and slippers that morning, five or six others running alongside him.

Hassan, lower on the slope, did not wait to reach for his slippers or his phone. He just ran, climbing a narrow, stair‑like path, up the hill, stopping only when he reached roughly 60 metres (200ft) above the road.

At some point, Miya and Hassan found each other. Around them were 60 to 70 other survivors who had also gathered high up on the hill.

A decade earlier, Miya had arrived in Syafrubesi as a carpenter. Three years later, he brought Hassan with him – both men from Bihar’s Bettiah district. Over the years, they built the town’s interiors – sofas, beds, almirahs, and kitchens for hotels and homes.

On that Wednesday morning, they watched all of that washed away. The multi‑storey hotels where they had worked – Red Panda, Garden Hotel, Buddha Hotel, Sunrise Hotel – were all swallowed by the flood.

“The town was gone in a blink,” Miya recounts, now sitting in his home in Turhapatti village of Bihar, India, just across the Nepal border. “There were only three kinds of people who survived that day: Those who were out of town, those who were at work and managed to run, and those who lived a little higher up the hill.”

Based on what he witnessed, Miya says only a few hundred people in Syafrubesi, a town that had a population of 2,271 in the 2011 census, likely survived.

Miya and Hasan are among them. Three of their close friends and colleagues, also migrant workers from Bihar, are not.

When the floods reached Syafrubesi, the men were already at work: Their shifts began at seven in the morning.

“To start at seven, we would wake up at four or five,” Miya recalls. They would leave with empty stomachs and were fed tea with doughnuts or biscuits at the construction site by building owners. Their first break came at 11am, when they returned to the rented one‑room space (3,500 Nepali rupees or $23 a month) that housed five to seven migrants at a time.

On the morning of August 26, they left for work alongside 34‑year‑old Arman Ansari, 20‑year‑old Samir Ansari, and 52‑year‑old Mukhtar Ansari, all migrants from Miya’s Turhapatti village.

In the rented room, two teenage boys, Arman’s 14‑year‑old son, Salman Alam, and his friend Shibu Alam, 17, remained asleep. They had come a month earlier to visit the hills.

“My father had cooked meat bhaat (rice with meat),” Salman recounts. He was waiting for his father to return at 11am so they could eat together.

Arman, his father, was working beside Hassan on the ground floor, pasting sunmica onto the same bed. Samir and Mukhtar were on the top floor of the Full Moon Hotel.

When Hassan ran out of the under-construction building and up the hill, he believed Arman was behind him. But by the time Hassan and Miya met higher up, there was no sign of the other three: Arman, Samir and Mukhtar.

Miya and Hassan found the boys, Salman and Shibu, terrified, on the hill. “Salman was crying, howling and searching for his father,” Hassan said.

The flood, which came with a high speed, took half an hour to recede. Soon, helicopters started hovering above them, airlifting the critically injured.

The four of them – Miya, Hassan and the boys – walked down the hill on foot to search for the three missing in the debris. They found nothing but sludge. Miya’s furniture-cutting tools and machines, worth 80,000 Nepali rupees ($530), were buried in the debris.

When they got back to their room, perched high on a slope, they found that it had survived.

But the army had taken charge, and soldiers herded survivors away from tenements near the river. “They said it [the flood] might come again,” Miya recalls.

They slept that night in a government school building in a village, he says. “At night, we were given daal bhat (rice and daal), and we wrapped ourselves in tarpaulin and slept.”

The next morning, a helicopter took them to another village. From there, another helicopter carried them to an army compound in a town. In the evening, they teamed up with five other migrants and hired an SUV to reach Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, each paying 3,500 rupees ($23).

The next morning, on August 28, they hired another SUV, which charged them 950 rupees ($6) each for a distance of 290km (180 miles) to Birgunj, a town on the India-Nepal border. They then crossed the border on foot before boarding buses for their villages.

It wasn’t the homecoming Indian migrants who work in Nepal usually plan.

Turhapatti is among thousands of villages tucked along the 1,715km (1,066-mile) stretch of the India-Nepal border, where generations have crossed back and forth in search of work.

The two countries share an open border, and on both sides, especially in Bihar, the bond is known as a roti-beti ka rishta (a relationship of food and daughters), alluding to ties of livelihoods and matrimonial kinship. People live, work, and marry across the border.

Kathmandu is as close to Turhapatti as is Patna, the capital of Bihar. Per its 2021 Population and Housing Census, Nepal had 700,000 foreign-born residents, 97 percent of them from India.

Miya and Hassan say the wages for a carpenter or a mason on the Indian side are between 600-700 rupees, while for the same work in Nepal, wages are about 900 rupees. That drives migrant workers from India over the border into Nepal.

Nepal, for its part, is facing a major out-migration crisis — its per capita income is the lowest in South Asia, barring Afghanistan, and hundreds of thousands of young men and women leave each year to find work elsewhere. This creates a demand for migrant workers from Bihar, India’s poorest state that lies just across the border.

In Turhapatti, Miya owns only 0.03 hectares (0.06 acres), not enough to feed his family of six children, wife and parents. In recent years, he transitioned from being a carpenter to a contractor, which allowed him to bring in more workers from Bihar.

He had been sending 30,000 Indian rupees ($315) back to his family every month.

Hassan has even less back home: He inherited a 6×8-metre (20×25ft) room from his father and no agricultural land. “There is no regular daily work here,” he says. He would send 15,000 Indian rupees ($157) home from Nepal each month for his wife and four children.

Their story echoes in most homes in Turhapatti. The village had a population of 16,000 people in the 2011 census, India’s latest one. In nearly every household, men have left to work in other parts of India and abroad as carpenters, masons, or labourers mixing cement and sand into mortar.

The destinations are Kashmir, where close to 700 men from the village work; Nepal, with nearly 600; and thousands scattered across Indian cities: Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai. About 100 men have migrated to Dubai, Oman and Saudi Arabia.

The houses they built in Turhapatti stand in stark contrast to those of those who remain in India. The marble-fronted and iron-gated homes belong to men working in the Gulf, while semi-permanent dwellings belong to those who stayed behind.

Migrants in Nepal fall in between: Miya has been able to raise a brick house.

This economic reality is what drove Arman Ansari to Syafrubesi. On July 26, Arman left for Nepal with Samir and Mukhtar. Arman’s son and his friend Shubu went with the three adults; the teenagers were on a trip to the hills.

Now, Arman’s brother-in-law. Jameel Miya, a carpenter in Kathmandu, scours the city’s hospitals for Arman’s body, telling authorities that his brother-in-law’s right hand and chest had deep scars, cut by shards of glass when he was young.

Arman’s wife, Sahrun Khatun, has only her last phone call with Arman to hold on to. They spoke two hours before the floods swept him away. “He was about to get his wages on September 1 and return home,” she says.

Salman, who had tagged along with his father to see the hills, hasn’t been able to sleep since the flood.

“The moment I close my eyes, I feel the flood is coming for me,” he says.

Mukhtar’s family lives a few lanes away.

Since the floods, Kasmun Khatun, Mukhtar’s wife, has been glued to the internet for any news of her missing husband. Joining her in that remote search are her daughter Asmana (18) and son Sadre Alam (14).

Her eldest son, Osama, 25, a tailor in Kathmandu, has been busy searching for his father in city hospitals.

“After waiting for a week and watching the videos, I submitted my DNA samples,” he says over a phone call. Osama manages to send home 6,000 rupees ($63), but that is no longer enough – his mother needs eye surgery that has already been delayed and cannot be put off much longer.

“The guardian has gone, all of a sudden,” he says, referring to his father.

At the far edge of Turhapatti stands the home of Samir Ansari, the youngest among the missing migrants and youngest of his five migrant brothers.

The Ganesh Hotel project he was working on was only three days from completion.

“He said he found another site to work on,” recalls his father, Hasmuddin Miya, remembering their last phone call on the evening of August 25.

Samir was a mason who specialised in marble tiles, a skill he had learned in Kashmir while working under his elder brothers at construction sites.

The three families are preparing to host a bhoj, the funeral feast – a custom of feeding hundreds of people – having given up on hope.

Meanwhile, the two survivors, Miya and Hassan, are already making calls to find work again. This time, their search turns towards Nepal’s plains. They pledge never to return to the hills.

“My whole body shivers at the thought of going there,” says Hassan.

articles.title: Biggest-ever Roman wall mosaic, featuring mysterious port city, revealed
articles.summary: The city of Rome has revealed for the first time the biggest Roman wall mosaic ever found, and a colorful fresco painted on a 2,000-year-old wall — the culmination of a massive 14-year restoration project.
articles.body: The city of Rome has revealed for the first time the biggest Roman wall mosaic ever found, and a colorful fresco painted on a 2,000-year-old wall — the culmination of a massive 14-year restoration project. Ten meters (33 feet) high and 16 meters (52 feet) long, the Great Mosaic, as it has been named, sits beneath the the Oppian Hill, where the emperor Nero built his famed golden house between 64 and 68 AD. “We estimate that it is the biggest wall mosaic ever found in the Roman World and we are still digging to find out where it stops,” archaeologist Francesco Pacetti said at the unveiling of the site on Tuesday. The archaeologists said it is unclear whether the mosaic, which also dates from the 1st century AD, was part of Nero’s lavish digs, or if it was built as part of a separate private dwelling that Nero eventually incorporated. The entire area, a stone’s throw from the Colosseum, was converted into public baths in 109 AD by the emperor Trajan, and the older Great Mosaic and the nearby “Painted City” fresco would have featured as a backdrop for bathers. Part of the mosaic, which was first discovered during excavations in the 1990s, could not be recovered, but what remains is a colorful scene. It depicts a walled-in port city from a bird’s eye view, complete with public squares and towers that were not common during the 1st century AD. The intricate details include blue and terracotta colors that have faded over time, depicting various scenes playing out in the port city — almost like a theatrical performance. At the top of the mosaic are close ups of various characters as if they are watching the action below in the port. They include a life-size bearded philosopher and his muse, several statues and a young poet, plus a theatrical stage with columns, garlands and vegetal swirls, all enhanced with blue and white marble and gemstones to create the effect of the sun shining on the sea. Experts don’t yet know whether the scenes represent a utopian port city or a real place in the ancient Roman world. “It could be a real place or an imagined city, we are not sure,” Pacetti said, adding that no known city has the same recognizable features, but that a port may have had them at the time when the mosaic was created. The newly restored “Painted City” fresco, which sits between two pillars at the entrance to the area where the mosaic was found, was also discovered during excavations in the 1990s. Also dated to the 1st century, the 10-square-meter (108-square-foot) fresco is as detailed as the mosaic, with scenes depicting a walled city, with a port entrance gate, roads, a theater and a temple. Archaeologists are currently working to expose another area of the mosaic, which shows a grape harvest and wine-making. The entire site, which encompasses the expansive 60,000-square-meter (15-acre) ruins of Trajan’s Baths and its exedra — a large semicircle supporting wall complete with cut-out shelves, suggesting the baths were also used as an ancient library — will soon be used to host book launches, in a nod to its original use as a library, Rome officials said. Viewing walkways have been installed, as well as lighting that helps reveal the intricate details of both the mosaic and the fresco. “We are giving this unique wonder back to the city,” Roberto Gualtieri, the mayor of Rome, said at the inauguration.

articles.title: Brooklyn teachers who witnessed 9/11 as children reveal what they want the next generation to remember
articles.summary: A Brooklyn principal watched a twin towers collapse from a school roof, not knowing her FDNY firefighter brother was underneath the rubble that day.
articles.body: When Americans mark 25 years since the 9/11 terrorist attacks on Friday, Kathleen Palladino will remember the day through the eyes of a New York City 6-year-old who did not yet understand what she was seeing. Palladino was a kindergartner in Brooklyn when classmates suddenly began being called over the school PA system to go home. Eventually, her mother arrived to collect Palladino and her older sister, and as they walked home, the little girl looked toward Manhattan. "It was like a dividing line," Palladino recently told Fox News Digital. "From the bridge backwards was just blackness." REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS The other side of the afternoon sky remained clear and blue. "Mommy, why is the sky black?" Palladino remembers asking. "She just kept squeezing my hand, and we just kept going," she said. A quarter-century later, Palladino teaches nursery school at St. Patrick Catholic Academy in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, where her 3-year-old students were born more than two decades after the attacks that shaped their teacher's childhood. She is one of several educators at the school whose memories of 9/11 stretch back to their own school days. As the nation remembers Friday, they are teaching children about an event that remains deeply personal to them but that their students know only as history. AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET Their principal, Kathy Curatolo, carries an even more personal connection — she watched one of the towers collapse from a school roof that morning, unaware her youngest brother, 31-year-old FDNY firefighter Robert Curatolo, was underneath it. For Palladino's young students, the lessons begin simply. "I don't go into the events of 9/11," she said. "They are too young, and the scope of what happened is just beyond their understanding right now." Instead, she teaches them what they can do when someone is hurting. "Can we clean up our toys without being asked? Can we go give them a hug?" she said. "Anything to show the ones that we love that we're here for them." MASSIVE PIECE OF 9/11 HISTORY MAKES STUNNING 10,500-MILE JOURNEY ACROSS AMERICA For fourth-grade teacher Elizabeth Giacchino, 9/11 begins in her memory with a ringing telephone. Giacchino was a sixth grader at Our Lady of Guadalupe School in Brooklyn when her teacher answered a call and told the class something had happened involving the Twin Towers. "So many of my classmates around me just started screaming and crying because they had family members that were working in the city," she said. Outside the window, Giacchino could see smoke. Parents began arriving, but Giacchino and her older sister remained because their mother worked at the school. "All I wanted to do was just be with my family at that time," she said. I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES Years later, after becoming a teacher herself, another memory took on new meaning. Giacchino remembered how calm her own teacher had remained while children cried around her. "I don't even know if she was feeling some type of way or if there was any personal situation she was going through, because all she thought about was us," Giacchino said. "So that's what I always make sure to do with my students too." Nikki Fregara, now a third-grade teacher at St. Patrick, was a high school senior when a phone call interrupted her first class of the day, history. "I hate to tell you all this, but I'm afraid that the Twin Towers got hit," she remembers her teacher saying. The students went to the window. "We saw the smoke," Fregara said. NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS She remembers crying and screaming in the hallway and students gathering in the auditorium around a small box television to watch the news. Fregara worried about her father, whose work took him to buildings around the city, and her sister and brother-in-law, who worked nearby. Today, she steers her third-graders away from the graphic details and toward the first responders who ran toward danger. "Helping others is so important, especially when they are in need," Fregara said. Her message to them is simple: "Never forget to be an everyday hero." For Curatolo, however, the hero she tells students about was her younger brother. Curatolo was headed to a principals' meeting on Sept. 11, 2001, when she heard on the radio that a plane had struck the World Trade Center. At the meeting, she and the other principals watched the second plane strike on TV before returning to their schools. 9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY Curatolo had four brothers, three firefighters and a police officer, and her mother initially called with reassuring news: all four were OK. Curatolo turned her attention to her students and eventually went onto the school roof. "I saw the second tower fall, not realizing that tower killed my brother," she said. Robert Curatolo had been an FDNY firefighter for six years and was assigned to Ladder 16 in Manhattan. Kathy said Robert had just gotten off duty when the attacks began and headed toward the World Trade Center with two other firefighters in a police car. One survived, allowing the family to later learn some of what Robert did that morning. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS Robert began directing dazed people away from falling debris, Kathy said. When the first building collapsed, he was in a walkway between the towers. Curatolo survived and then returned to the rubble. Kathy said her family learned that Robert pulled a man with two broken legs through the debris and into the street. When the second tower collapsed, Robert dove beneath a fire truck, she said, but it could not withstand the collapse. People have asked Kathy why he didn't leave after surviving once. "That's not who he was," she said. "That's not how we were raised." Yet that is not the only Robert she wants her students to know. The youngest of eight siblings, Robert was funny, easygoing and athletic. He loved movies and traveling and was, Kathy remembers, almost always late. "So he actually ended up at the Trade Center on time, where we're like, the only thing you ever got to on time," she said. Robert had married at Disney World just three weeks before 9/11. The wedding was the last time Kathy saw him, though she spoke to him by phone the day before he died. "I want them to know that Robert was — he was a regular kid growing up just like them," she said. Curatolo remembers realizing around the 10th anniversary that students increasingly had no memory of 9/11. "These kids have no idea what I'm talking about unless they learn it from us in school or their parents who had experienced something," she said. Today, she said, children accustomed to smartphones and instantaneous communication are astonished to learn survivors sometimes couldn't contact their families. She tells them about grounded planes, postponed baseball games and packed churches and remembers that after the attacks, "people were kinder to each other." Twenty-five years later, Curatolo said she also wants students to understand that remembering tragedy does not mean allowing it to define a life. "My brother is always with me, but I don't let 9/11 define me," she said. "You can survive a tragedy and still live a good life because the people who were lost don't want you to stop living your life." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Her family continues to honor Robert through a scholarship foundation, charitable work and support for Tunnel to Towers. Kathy still counts him among the eight Curatolo siblings. "There are eight of us," she said. "Four live in Florida, three live on Staten Island, and one's in heaven."

articles.title: Love is Blind couple on ADHD and life in Guernsey
articles.summary: A couple who appeared on the Netflix show tell of their "amazing" life in the bailiwick.
articles.body:
A couple who appeared in a reality dating show have told of their "amazing" life in Guernsey one year after they first met on the show.

Jack Bradshaw, 30, and Faye Domaille, 28, featured in series three of Netflix's Love is Blind: UK, and have remained together despite the show's low success rate .

The format sees singles date each other in pods but they are separated by a wall. They can only see one another after they get engaged, and then have to navigate a honeymoon, moving in together, meeting families, and a legally binding wedding.

During the show psychologists helped Bradshaw come to terms with having ADHD. The pair have since moved in with Domaille's parents in St Saviour.

Bradshaw, from Cornwall, said life had been "brilliant" and Guernsey "feels like home".

"Cornwall will always be my home but there's something about Guernsey - it's been amazing," he told BBC Radio Guernsey.

"There's similar seaside, countryside vibes, but everything here is so close together."

He said: "I've started playing for Sylvan's football club, and Faye's parents have been so welcoming.

"I've adjusted to island life so well, and now it just feels like home."

Domaille had been based in London for five years before she featured on the show, and said moving home to Guernsey "was not the plan".

"I was really keen to get back to London, but we decided to go travelling and use up all our savings, which was insane, although I have no regrets."

One area the couple said they had grown the most was in understanding Bradshaw's ADHD diagnosis .

A psychologist on the show said Bradshaw exhibited the traits of someone with the condition.

"I spent my entire life refusing to admit that I had ADHD," he said.

"But, since I met Faye and starting having conversations about it, it has given me such clarity as to why I do certain things and why my brain works in a different way."

Bradshaw said he had been "overwhelmed" by the number of people sending him positive messages about his story.

"People have said their children love themselves a little bit more after seeing me the TV, which I never imagined, so that's something I would like to talk about and build a community around."

Domaille said: "The biggest thing is just being patient with each other, and I see Jack's ADHD as a superpower.

"He is the funniest person I've ever met and we are genuinely in fits of laughter almost 100% of the time."

She said life has been a rollercoaster, but that she "loves researching" ADHD.

"When he does something, I'll be confused; but will then search it online and realise it's something common for someone with ADHD to do, and then it makes sense."

Domaille went on to say the hardest part of the Love Is Blind "experiment" was being thrown back "into the real world" without the show's welfare team and financial support.

"Sometimes some of the toughest parts in the experiment are when you have to have genuine conversations about where you're going to live and what kind of jobs you're going to have.

"We're very fortunate in our season everyone's still together, but that's not the same for a lot of the seasons in the US and the UK.

"People often don't make it through that year and it really highlights what marriage is actually really about, and it's not always sunshine and roses."

articles.title: Iceland to propose whaling ban, leaving Norway and Japan isolated
articles.summary: Iceland’s government will submit a bill to ban whaling, a move that would leave Norway and Japan as the only two countries to continue commercial whaling.
articles.body: Iceland’s government will submit a bill in ​February to ban whaling, a move that would leave Norway and Japan as the only two countries in the world to continue commercial whaling. Whaling in Iceland has ⁠sparked years of protests from animal welfare campaigners and Hollywood celebrities. The bill will include “a permanent ban on whaling,” the government, which has a majority in parliament, said on its website late on Wednesday. In this ⁠year’s hunting season, which runs ​from ⁠June to around the end of September, 80 fin whales were caught as of September 9, according to ⁠Humane World for Animals, an animal welfare group that tracks ​the ⁠catches. The quota allows ‌150 fin whales to be killed this year. “There is considerable political and public support for this bill to ban commercial whaling, ‌and compelling ethical, veterinary, legal and conservation ‌reasons to hope it succeeds,” said Wendy Higgins, a Humane World for Animals spokeswoman. Fin whales, the primary target of Iceland’s whaling industry, are classified ⁠by the International Union for Conservation of Nature as vulnerable. In 2024, Iceland’s interim government issued a five-year license to its sole remaining whaling company. Only Iceland, Norway and Japan have conducted commercial whaling in recent years, according to the International Whaling Commission’s catch list. Norway resumed commercial whaling in 1993 and Iceland in 2006, ‌despite an international moratorium that took effect in 1986 ​to protect whale populations. Japan withdrew from the International ‌Whaling Commission in 2019 and ⁠resumed commercial whaling in its territorial waters and exclusive ⁠economic zone. The moratorium allows indigenous peoples in certain parts of the world, such ‌as Greenland and ​Alaska, to hunt whales because whale ‌products play a vital role ​in their nutritional and cultural lives.

articles.title: Kemi Badenoch denies housing benefit cuts plan would make people homeless
articles.summary: The Conservatives say £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill to help fund increased defence spending.
articles.body:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has denied her party's plans to cut housing benefit would make people homeless, but suggested some would have to "move somewhere cheaper".

At Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, she had challenged Andy Burnham to commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying the cost could be covered by cuts to welfare.

The Conservatives have claimed £4bn could be cut from the housing benefit bill, in part by allowing tenancies in areas where housing is expensive to come to an end.

Asked whether she would be willing to make people homeless in order to fund defence, Badenoch told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the party would "protect existing tenants".

During PMQs, Burnham argued national security "can't come at the expense of social security".

He repeated that a target date for increasing defence spending to 3% of GDP would be announced in the spending review in the spring.

The PM insisted he would get the welfare bill down in "the Labour way", by boosting council housebuilding, supporting young people into work and providing more mental health support.

National security can't come at expense of social security, Burnham says

Badenoch accuses Burnham of kicking defence spending into the long grass

Badenoch said the government should cut housing benefit to fund defence spending now, adding she would exempt pensioners and existing tenants from the plans.

Speaking on the Today programme, she said: "What we're doing is making sure that people are protected, but capping the amount that people get on benefits because we need to look after our national security.

"Without national security, there aren't going to be any benefits. We're all going to be in danger, far more people will be homeless, and the government's first duty is defence of the realm."

Her proposed changes would be part of a package that would cut £23bn from welfare to partly fund an increase in defence spending.

Housing benefit can be paid to people who are unemployed or on a low income to help cover the cost of rent, with the rate varying by council area.

The number of people eligible to claim housing benefit has increased by more than one million since 2020, driven by the soaring cost of private rents.

The total cost of housing benefit is forecast to hit £39bn this year, according to the Department for Work and Pensions, driven by the increasing number of claimants.

In an interview with BBC Breakfast, Badenoch was asked who would be affected by her plans to cut housing benefit.

She said: "We have people who live in areas that are quite expensive and if people need local housing allowance they will need to move somewhere cheaper.

"I think you should aspire to live wherever you want to live, but you shouldn't aspire for the government, i.e. other taxpayers, to pay for you to live wherever you want to live...

"We're not removing people from homes - this doesn't cover pensioners, it doesn't affect existing tenants - but I do think you need to be fair."

Responding to Badenoch at PMQs, Burnham said the policy would worsen homelessness and end up costing the government more.

He said: "I don't think, myself, that taking £4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation."

articles.title: How Ukraine’s deepest attack in Russia, on Arctic gas, signals new reach
articles.summary: Long-range Ukrainian drones hit Russia’s key gas plants, raising questions about the conflict’s next phase.
articles.body:
Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border, on Wednesday, signalling that Ukraine has further developed its military capabilities as the Russia-Ukraine war continues through its fifth year.

Unconfirmed videos circulating on social media show large clouds of thick, dark smoke and fire at the Novy Urengoy plant in western Siberia, recorded from a distance. Dmitry Artyukhov, the governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug region, wrote on Telegram that the drone attacks had been intercepted and “debris from the drone caused a fire upon impact”. There have been no reports of deaths or injuries.

Since the start of the war, Ukraine has dramatically increased its capacity for the mass production of low-cost drones and has more recently been specifically targeting Russia’s energy infrastructure and logistical hubs.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the latest long-range attack “completely justified” on social media. It came just days after special United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv with new proposals to end the war, although no specific details were shared on the new proposals.

While attacks on Russia’s and Ukraine’s capitals were halted during the three-day visit earlier this week, they immediately resumed following their departure.

But what does this new, long-range capability on Ukraine’s side mean for the next phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war?

What do we know about the Ukrainian drones used in the strike?

The Ukrainian Armed Forces says it hit two critical Russian gas processing plants, in Novy Urengoy and Purovsky district, with FP-1 drones produced by Fire Point, a Ukrainian company specialising in the production of long-range drones.

The pink FP-1 drone – Fire Point FP-1 UAV – is about 6 metres (20ft) wide and can travel at 140-180km (87-112 miles) per hour. It costs less than $60,000 to produce each drone, an amount that is considered low.

The furthest an FP-1 drone had travelled before the Novy Urengoy attack was in July, when it hit an oil refinery in the city of Omsk in southwestern Siberia, about 2,500km (1,550 miles) from the border with Ukraine.

The Kremlin’s envoy to the Urals, Artem Zhoga, said Wednesday’s attack by Ukraine was the first to reach the Arctic.

The targets were two Russian gas processing plants in the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky districts of Yamalo-Nenets.

The Yamalo-Nenets region hosts about 80 percent of Russia’s natural gas production and two-thirds of its gas reserves, as well as 13 percent of the country’s oil reserves. Gas reserves in this region stand at 26.5 trillion cubic metres; global gas needs stand at about 4.2 trillion cubic metres per year.

Novy Urengoy is known as the gas capital of Russia due to its vital production for the Russian gas and oil industry.

The ability of Ukraine to reach targets here means it could unleash much more damage on Russia’s economy, which depends heavily on energy exports for income – especially as Russia has been under international economic and trade sanctions since it first invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Videos of Russian citizens queueing for petrol were shared widely on social media earlier this year, despite Russia holding one of the world’s largest reserves of gas and oil.

The attack on Russian gas infrastructure could have serious consequences for the European Union as member states heavily depend on supplies of Russian gas.

Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the EU implemented sanctions on Russian oil and gas and began to invest in efforts to become less reliant on Russian energy.

But the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which previously moved about 20 percent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, means that Europe is once again struggling for gas imports.

Gas prices in Europe rose above 80 euros ($93) per megawatt-hour this week, the highest price since 2023, according to the Dutch TTF, a wholesale market that sets the price benchmark for European gas.

Current gas reserves in Europe stand at about 65 percent, compared with 80 percent last year, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Dwindling reserves are currently a particular worry for the continent as it heads into winter.

EU member states were urged to start storing gas in March, shortly after the US and Israel started the war on Iran. But the European Court of Auditors released a report on Wednesday stating that member states have not invested enough in other energy sources to be able to phase out Russian gas, and that the bloc’s “crisis‑response objectives often cannot be demonstrated”.

articles.title: Key takeaways from the GOP midterm convention and a first look at the iPhone Duo: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Trump tries to energize his base with a $5,000 promise.
articles.body: Trump tries to energize his base with a $5,000 promise. Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer said she rejects the conspiracy theories about her ex-husband. And a hands-on look at the new foldable iPhone. Here’s what to know today. Trump makes the midterms about him in GOP convention speech: ‘I’m on the ballot’ President Donald Trump sought to energize Republican voters in a keynote speech during the party’s first-ever midterm convention, imploring supporters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” His name is not on the ballot in November, but he said his supporters need to vote like it is as the GOP fights to keep control of the House and Senate. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Trump’s approval ratings, however, are at an all-time low, and the party is worried about MAGA voters not turning out in large numbers. Trump said roughly 35 seats in both the House and the Senate are considered tossups, and he pledged to hold events in all of those races. He also promised that his administration would hand out $5,000 dividend checks to Americans if Republicans hold on to Congress, though he said the money would have to be spent in the U.S. He didn’t specify where the roughly $1.35 trillion needed would come from or how spending would be enforced. He told supporters that the Iran war, now in its seventh month, would be over “very shortly after the election.” The event in Dallas is designed to put the president front and center in the closing stages of the midterm election cycle. Indeed, Trump has so far been the star of the show. Speakers yesterday mentioned his name 155 times, and Trump invoked his own name 16 times. The only other word mentioned more was variations of “America.” The mood inside the convention arena. More politics news: Sen. John Fetterman made a surprise cameo at the GOP convention, calling himself a “common-sense Democrat” and praising GOP Sen. Dave McCormick. Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee lost his Democratic primary to former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, becoming the first governor to fall in a primary this year and the first in eight years. And Providence Mayor Brett Smiley lost his Democratic primary, with state Rep. David Morales, a Bernie Sanders-endorsed democratic socialist, prevailing. For subscribers: The Defense Department’s powerful second in command has found himself entangled in the unusual and very public case of an arrested CIA officer found with $40 million worth of gold bars stored at his home. For subscribers: The sizable cash gifts Trump made to Natalie Harp and three other White House aides present ethical and legal concerns about whether he was trying to supplement their salaries, experts said. Lindsay Clancy rejects conspiracy theories about her ex-husband, lawyer says In a wide-ranging interview with NBC News, Lindsay Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington rejected the conspiracy theories accusing Clancy’s ex-husband of killing their three children and said Clancy talks about her children, often repeating the phrase, “I want my babies.” Reddington said Clancy is aware of how her case has taken off on social media. “She knows, and it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop,” Reddington said. Both the prosecution and defense in Clancy’s trial admitted she killed her children: Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months old. But “that was not the Lindsay that is now living among us,” Reddington said. Since last week’s mistrial, Clancy is “not very good” and remains “suicidal,” Reddington said, adding that she’s on “24/7, one-on-one suicide watch. I worry about her every day.” See more from the interview. Hands-on with Apple’s iPhone Duo Apple unveiled its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, the biggest change to the company’s smartphone since it was first introduced nearly 20 years ago. There’s the external screen, as any normal smartphone has — but open it up, and users will see a 7.6-inch display that allows for two apps to run side-by-side or for a bigger streaming video experience. NBC News chief tech analyst Joanna Stern played with the Duo for an hour after Apple’s event. “My first impression? This feels like a turning point in iPhone history,” she wrote. In comparison to other foldable phones that came before it, the iPhone Duo is thin, and the internal screen lacks a crease, Stern noted. But one of the biggest advantages of the $1,999 device is the software, not its shape, she said. Stern shares more of her first impressions. ‘Once-in-a-millennium moment’: Medieval masterpiece Bayeux Tapestry finally goes on show in London The 230-foot Bayeux Tapestry, which tells the story of William the Conqueror’s 1066 invasion of England, finally went on show to the public in London’s British Museum today. It reflects a “really seismic moment in British history,” the project’s curator said. Tickets sold out long in advance of its public opening. NBC News was given exclusive access to the work, which was transported earlier this year to London from France in a secretive, high-tech operation. Staff Pick : Why jet lag could decide the NFL’s first game in Australia The NFL is a copycat league, where one successful strategy is quickly adopted by other teams. (See the “Tush Push.”) And you can be sure the other 30 teams will be watching today to see whether the San Francisco 49ers or Los Angeles Rams look fresher when they play in Melbourne, Australia. The NFL will play a record nine international games this season as it tries to expand its reach globally. For teams, that means increasingly long-haul travel. In the case of the 49ers and Rams, each sought to battle the jet lag from their 17-hour flight to Australia in wildly different ways. I talked to sleep experts to hear the pros and cons for both teams’ strategies — and maybe it will even help your preparation for your next long flight, too. — Andrew Greif, sports reporter Read All About It Extensive recovery efforts have begun in Kauai after Hurricane Lowell lifted a house off its foundation, split another in two and left thousands without power. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s move to tamp down rising bond yields backfired after his department announced that it would repurchase $6 billion in government bonds. The Seattle Seahawks squeezed past the New England Patriots 13-10 in the NFL season opener, but their title defense took a hit, not least with the injury to star quarterback Sam Darnold. For subscribers: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a political storm after a bombshell news report alleged that he had advanced warning about the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks and chose not to alert security officials. Plus, now’s a good time to make sure you’re cleaning your reusable water bottle properly. Here’s how to keep yours free of grime, mold and other harmful bacteria, according to microbiology experts. Today’s newsletter was curated for you by Elizabeth Robinson. If you’re a fan, please send a link to your family and friends. They can sign up here.

articles.title: In the 1970s, Johnny Cash bought a 107-acre Tennessee hideaway. After he died in 2003, the abandoned farm became a music museum
articles.summary: US News: For nearly three decades, Johnny Cash had a place in Bon Aqua, Tennessee, where life moved at a quieter pace than the recording studios and stages he .
articles.body: For nearly three decades, Johnny Cash had a place in Bon Aqua, Tennessee, where life moved at a quieter pace than the recording studios and stages he knew so well. The 107-acre property became a private retreat for Cash and his wife, June Carter Cash, after he found it in the early 1970s. He used the farm as a place to garden, cook, read, write and spend time away from public life. After Cash died in 2003, the property was left unused and gradually deteriorated. More than a decade later, new owners began bringing it back. Today, the former hideaway is open to visitors, with the farmhouse and surrounding property preserving a lesser-known part of Cash’s life.How Johnny Cash turned his Bon Aqua farm into a peaceful retreatCash’s connection with the Tennessee countryside developed during a period when his professional life was already closely tied to the state. He performed and recorded in Nashville and Memphis, while Bon Aqua offered something considerably removed from the demands of his career.The property came into his possession during a complicated period involving his finances. Cash discovered in the 1970s that his accountant had been embezzling money and had acquired real estate in Cash’s name. After the situation was uncovered, Cash and June Carter Cash took control of the properties. Most were eventually sold, but the Bon Aqua farm remained.Cash later described the place as somewhere he could simply live at his own pace. He wrote about tending a garden, preparing his own meals, reading and walking across the land. It was also a setting where he could think and work without the constant movement associated with his music career. For Cash, the farm was more than another piece of property.How a small Tennessee community became part of Johnny Cash’s private worldThe Bon Aqua home was used by Cash and June Carter Cash for years, and the property became part of their private routine. Cash also developed a connection with the nearby community.A local general store became an unlikely part of that story. Cash would sometimes perform there for people in the area, giving informal shows rather than the large-scale concerts associated with his career. Some of those performances later became part of the material preserved at the museum.The property therefore carries two sides of Cash’s life. The farmhouse represents the private retreat, while the nearby store recalls his willingness to perform in an ordinary local setting.The ranch was left empty after Cash diedCash died in 2003, and the Bon Aqua property subsequently stood unused. Without regular care, the farmhouse and other parts of the site fell into disrepair.The property eventually attracted Brian and Sally Oxley, who purchased it in 2015 for $895,000, as reported by The Tennessean.Brian Oxley had not grown up listening to Cash and was unfamiliar with much of his music when he first encountered the ranch. His interest changed after hearing Cash’s later recordings, including the American Recordings material. When the Bon Aqua property came onto the market, the couple decided to buy it.The farmhouse preserved Cash’s most personal memoriesThe farmhouse still contained items connected with Cash and his family. Among the discoveries were guitars, personal material and a VHS recording of one of the informal performances at the nearby convenience store.There was also a car with a connection to Cash’s song “One Piece at a Time”. The vehicle was inspired by the idea at the centre of the 1976 song, in which a worker assembles a car by gradually bringing its parts home.The farmhouse itself offered smaller reminders of family life. Bullet holes remained in one wall from an occasion when Cash taught his daughter Cindy how to shoot. Details such as these are less polished than the memorabilia normally associated with a major music star, but they provide a glimpse into how the property was actually used.The Oxleys later acquired the nearby convenience store as well, allowing another piece of Cash’s Bon Aqua story to remain connected to the farm.Restoration turned the hideaway into a public museumThe restoration began in earnest after the Oxleys bought the property. The aim was not simply to preserve a house but to create a place where visitors could encounter Cash’s connection to Bon Aqua.The site eventually opened as the Storytellers Museum in 2016. Displays inside the farmhouse brought together period furnishings, handwritten material, letters, guitars, lyrics and other objects associated with Cash.Some of the material relates directly to his time in the area. One example is the song “Saturday Night in Hickman County”, which drew inspiration from Cash’s regular appearances at the Bon Aqua convenience store.The museum also continued the connection between the property and live music. Performances could be held at the old shop, echoing the informal shows Cash had once given there.The site now preserves Cash’s private connection to TennesseeThe property is now known as Hideaway Farm, a name Cash used himself. Restoration added visitor facilities, while the farmhouse preserves a quieter side of his life through surviving belongings and personal spaces. The site also includes the American Garage, featuring music memorabilia linked to Elvis Presley and Colonel Tom Parker. For Cash, Bon Aqua was more than a retreat. It was a place to garden, write, cook, read and escape the demands of his career. Today, the restored farm offers a glimpse into that private side of his life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: At least 20 dead and 5 missing after cargo ship catches fire in Chinese port, state media says
articles.summary: At least 20 people were killed and five were missing after a cargo ship caught fire while docked in a Chinese port, Chinese state media reported Thursday.
articles.body: At least 20 people were killed and five were missing after a cargo ship caught fire while docked in a Chinese port, Chinese state media reported Thursday. The ship was docked for repairs in the Beihai Shipbuilding Co. at the port of Qingdao, a major shipping hub on the northeastern Chinese coast. A photo released by Xinhua news agency identified the ship as the Ocean Melody, which sails under a Liberian flag, according to the tracking website VesselFinder. A total of 42 people had been on the vessel, and 12 of them were safely evacuated, Xinhua reported. Five were injured and taken to the hospital, and they remained in a stable condition. The fire started around 11 a.m. Thursday and was extinguished by 2:30 p.m. local time. China’s President Xi Jinping issued “important instructions” to urgently conduct rescues of missing people on the ship, Xinhua said, adding that Premier Li Qiang called for “trapped” people to be rescued.

articles.title: European founders and VCs urge lawmakers 'to get EU Inc right' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amid negotiations for a new EU-wide corporate status, an open letter signed by unicorn founders and investors warns that 'EU Inc' shouldn’t be watered down.
articles.body:
Europe could soon have its own equivalent of the Delaware C Corp, but its advocates aren’t releasing the pressure on lawmakers. In an open letter released on Thursday, a who’s who of Europe’s startup scene stressed that this new corporate status shouldn’t be watered down.

The letter is the latest step of the EU Inc campaign, a movement calling for an EU-wide company statute that would let companies incorporate under a common framework and operate across the bloc. Its promoters have secured endorsements from the European Union’s top authorities, but now are expressing concern that the final legislation could become “unusable if its central features are weakened.”

As usual with European lawmaking, various national lobbies have entered the chat, including Germany’s notaries , whose association has criticized aspects of the European Commission’s proposal . But negotiations are still ongoing for the European Parliament and Council to settle on a final text, and EU Inc’s promoters are pointing out what’s at stake.

With some 100 days left before European institutions shut down for winter recess, the letter calls on policymakers to preserve the proposal, saying it the potential to “remove much of the friction and fragmentation that continue to throttle European companies, unlock investment and spur a new wave of entrepreneurship.”

Taking a page from older lobbies, the letter highlights points that “may seem like technical details, but […] separate a company form founders use from one they ignore.” In particular, they insist on one central registry; and that employees should be taxed only when they actually dispose of their stock options.

This need to get into the weeds isn’t new. In 2024, when original petition was gaining steam, Index Ventures partner and EU Inc supporter Martin Mignot told TechCrunch that “the devil is in the details, and that’s going to be where we’re going to be very, very watchful.”

EU Inc has also stepped up its namedropping game. On the investor side, EU Inc’s new letter has been signed by VCs including Accel partner Sonali De Rycker, Sequoia partner Michael Moritz, and Atomico founder Niklas Zennström — one of many tech figures who’s been supporting the campaign by sporting its cap .

To add gravitas on the entrepreneur side, promoters also highlighted endorsements from founders behind unicorns including Alan, ElevenLabs, Lovable, Mistral, and Synthesia. Some of these have their HQs in the United States; reading between the lines, the message to lawmakers is also that if EU Inc has its way, this could be a thing of the past.

articles.title: Algeria says cutting diplomatic ties with UAE
articles.summary: Relations have been strained for years, as the two countries took differing positions on several regional issues.
articles.body:
Algeria says it has decided ⁠to cut diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates after what it described as a series of “provocative or hostile” actions by Abu Dhabi despite “repeated warnings”.

Algeria’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that ⁠the UAE’s actions had reached a point where they could no longer be considered acceptable and that it had “exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations.”

It said the Emirati ambassador had been summoned to the ministry, informed of the decision and given 48 hours to comply.

There was no immediate comment from the UAE.

Relations between the two countries have come under growing strain in recent years, and Algiers and Abu Dhabi have taken differing positions on several regional issues.

Algeria opposes normalisation with Israel, while the UAE and Algeria’s regional rival Morocco established diplomatic ties with Israel under the United States-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020.

The two countries are also on opposing sides of the decades-old Western Sahara dispute. The UAE supports Morocco’s claim to sovereignty over the territory where it has a consulate, while Algeria backs the Polisario Front, which seeks an independent Western Sahara.

The two countries’ interests have increasingly intersected in the Sahel, where the UAE has expanded ties with several governments in recent years, while Algeria’s relations with some of its southern neighbours have become strained following a series of military coups.

Algerian President Abdelmajid Tebboune has often referred to the UAE in speeches as a “micro-state” or “statelet” seeking to destabilise several countries in the region.

“Wherever they set foot, blood flows,” he said in a televised interview in July, adding that the UAE has had a “very negative impact”.

“We want them to stay away, so that blood does not flow in our country,” he added.

At the time, Tebboune said a diplomatic break “would have happened long ago” had Algeria not sought to avoid “deepening divisions” in the Arab world.

articles.title: “I gotta be the first”: IShowSpeed makes history with iPhone Duo stunt at Apple event
articles.summary: US Streamers News: IShowSpeed turned Apple's new iPhone Duo event into a viral moment after deciding to perform a backflip while holding the company's first foldable iPh.
articles.body: IShowSpeed turned Apple's new iPhone Duo event into a viral moment after deciding to perform a backflip while holding the company's first foldable iPhone. The 21-year-old streamer was standing in front of new Apple CEO John Ternus when he suddenly said he wanted to be the first person to do a backflip with the device. Speed then completed the stunt without dropping the expensive phone, creating a funny and unexpected moment at Apple's major product event.IShowSpeed turns Apple’s iPhone Duo launch into a history-making backflipIShowSpeed was not happy with simply holding and testing Apple's brand-new iPhone Duo. articles.title: Hundreds of thousands lack adequate shelter at Sudan’s Tawila camp
articles.summary: Insufficient aid and shelter increase hardship for displaced in Tawila, as malnutrition and disease spread rapidly.
articles.body:
Blue tents stand in tight rows at the Daba Naira camp in Tawila, 68 kilometres west of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur in Sudan, racked by war.

The tents were set up by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), with support from the Turkish Disaster and Emergency Management Authority.

Relief teams have erected 3,000 new tents in recent months, but the number is negligible compared with the needs of more than 665,000 displaced people, the IOM said in a statement.

The most pressing question remains: how can this number of tents possibly be enough for hundreds of thousands of displaced people, especially when rainfall threatens to turn the low‑lying ground into swamps?

Abdelbagi Mohamed Hamid, the minister of social welfare and humanitarian affairs coordinator in the Darfur region, told Al Jazeera Arabic that the regional government appealed to donors, including the Turkish ambassador, to provide tents for the displaced.

As a result, Turkiye allocated 30,000 tents to be distributed in Darfur and Kordofan through the IOM. Abdelbagi said 3,000 of 6,000 expected tents were erected in the Daba Naira camp in Tawila. Another 2,450 were delivered to the Salam, al‑Wihda and al‑Nakheel camps in Shaeria locality in South and East Darfur.

The minister said the Malha locality had the greatest need for humanitarian assistance in Darfur, followed by Tina, Karnoy and Um Baru areas. The Tina border crossing should be opened to allow the delivery of aid to these isolated areas, which suffer from acute shortages of food, medicine and fuel, while the war has deepened their isolation and worsened their humanitarian situation, he said.

Abdelbagi warned that providing shelter alone is not enough to confront the crisis, given the looming danger of famine, which could prove deadlier than the war itself, as humanitarian organisations struggle to reach many affected regions.

The arrival of the new tents coincided with the beginning of the rainy season and an outbreak of fires sweeping through displacement camps, increasing the suffering of displaced people living under tattered canopies without protection from wind and rain, amid acute shortages of food, clean water and healthcare.

The IOM warned of persistent and worsening humanitarian needs in Tawila, as services deteriorate and diseases like cholera spread amid a lack of clean drinking water, resulting in watery diarrhoea and skin infections. The camps are overcrowded and lack basic sanitation.

The organisation, while continuing to expand the number of shelters in the Daba Naira camp, cannot keep up with the rapid pace of displacement.

Ahmed Mousa, a displaced man from el-Fasher who is staying in the Daba Naira camp, told Al Jazeera that the new tents do not cover even a tenth of the camp’s needs, with people sleeping in the rain in the open and children falling ill without adequate care.

Fatima Ibrahim, a displaced woman in the same camp, said people fled el-Fasher in search of safety – only to find themselves exposed to the elements, hunger and disease.

“We see the new tents from afar, but they are not enough. We are dropping like flies from hunger and disease. Our children fall ill before our eyes, and we don’t even have medicine,” she said, adding that many families slept on bare ground without protection from the cold of night and the heat of day.

The Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Darfur region, Al‑Sadiq Barango, told Al Jazeera in a statement that the famine may be more dangerous than the war, amid declining seasonal rains and the drying of agricultural lands and livestock pastures.

He says the war has driven farmers to abandon their land, while cultivated areas, particularly fruit farms and cash‑crop plantations, have been attacked and destroyed by armed groups.

Barango described the situation as “ominous signs of a looming catastrophe,” and called for urgent humanitarian intervention, as starvation threatens thousands of people across Sudan, with Darfur the most affected due to years of conflict and the collapse of agricultural infrastructure.

Tawila hosts about 665,000 displaced people, most of whom fled el-Fasher and its surroundings, according to the IOM’s statement. Their number had more than doubled between March and September 2025, from 238,000 to more than 652,000.

More than 70 percent of households in Tawila lack healthcare, while half of families have been unable to obtain treatment, according to the organisation’s estimates. Children under the age of five and pregnant women are the most affected, with rising rates of malnutrition and infectious diseases.

Adam Rijal, spokesperson for the Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees, told Al Jazeera that “Tawila is not just numbers,” noting that needs exceed capacities dozens of times over, and warning of more deaths, especially among children and the elderly, due to hunger, disease and the absence of basic services.

Humanitarian organisations face major difficulties reaching displaced people because of rough terrain and the spread of checkpoints belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which is at war with the Sudanese government and controls vital routes in the area.

Local activists say that aid trucks are sometimes subjected to looting and extortion, which raises the cost of relief and delays its arrival to those who need it. Many displaced people – according to field reports – have been forced to walk long distances to obtain limited food rations, while others go weeks without assistance.

In Tawila, where hundreds of thousands live in worn‑out tents amid disease outbreaks and the hazards of the rainy season, the need for shelter, food and care is growing, while 3,000 tents are nowhere near enough to confront a humanitarian catastrophe that is worsening by the day.
